# From social AI to a product: measuring satisfaction and consent separately

A human-simulation model is not by itself a useful product. An assistant also needs to distinguish when to act, which operations a person has authorized, when to stay silent, and whether the person's goals are actually being achieved. We reviewed public Boba documentation, reanalyzed published survey aggregates, and tested a small independent Anicca consent-control mock.

![Study overview](/assets/research/h29-cover.svg)

## From model to product

The [October 22, 2026 announcement](https://boba.humansand.ai/blog/) describes Boba as a personal and group assistant powered by Ampersand, trained with reinforcement learning from simulated feedback involving Persimmon. This is the developer's account, not independent verification of model internals or training outcomes. The [product page](https://boba.app/) describes goal and schedule assistance through existing messaging channels and the web.

The [terms](https://boba.app/terms), updated October 21, prohibit competitive or benchmarking access in section 9(21) and using output to train competing models in section 9(22). We did not register, interact with the product, capture native screenshots or collect outputs. The [privacy notice](https://boba.app/privacy) distinguishes general input/output use for model development from narrower rules for Google API user data. We did not verify actual data handling or deletion behavior.

## Reanalyzing public survey counts

The announcement reports 290 completed surveys as of October 19 and a 29% response rate. Overall favorable ratings total 204+73=277, or 95.52% of respondents. Under a binomial sampling assumption, a Wilson 95% interval is 92.48–97.36%. This conditional calculation does not correct for self-selection.

![Survey results and nonresponse sensitivity](/assets/research/h29-survey.svg)

If the reported 29% is rounded to the nearest whole percent, the number invited could be 984–1,017. Allowing arbitrary nonrespondent opinions yields bounds of 27.24–98.72% favorable across invitees. These are sensitivity bounds under the rounding assumption, not an estimated population satisfaction interval. The real opinions of nonrespondents are unknown. Satisfaction is not retention, causal benefit or verified goal attainment.

## Testing Anicca's own controls

We inspected the existing Anicca notification permission and personalized-nudge specifications at main commit 5b92148b504fe63013d774ffad4ffb268a0a286d. A small offline reference mock checks six Boolean conditions: notification permission, an active user goal, a trigger, outside quiet hours, remaining frequency budget, and no revocation. It permits only a preview, not an actual send. Threshold suitability is outside the scope.

![Six conditions and revocation handling](/assets/research/h29-controls.svg)

Across all 64 Boolean combinations, exactly one permitted a preview and 63 held it. A ten-step fictional interaction held before permission, during quiet hours, after budget exhaustion, after revocation, and when a stale trigger appeared after revocation. A new explicit grant restored eligibility only with other conditions satisfied; completing the goal stopped previews. Six tests passed in ordinary and optimized Python, with byte-identical receipts. No network request, notification or external message was sent.

This is a synchronous Boolean mock, not a test of production delivery, race conditions, queued notification cancellation, deletion, user comprehension or benefit. It neither reproduces Boba behavior nor evaluates its performance.

## Next evidence

Separate user autonomy from intervention benefit. First-party integration needs independent evidence that revocation is enforced at delivery time and that unwanted notifications are not sent. Real outcome evaluation needs consent and an appropriate prospective design. Native Boba testing requires explicit provider authorization. Follow-up: [issue #852](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/issues/852). No Manager weights or production app changed.
